title: The Smell of Soup and the Sound of Money
full_text:
One chilly winter afternoon in the bustling marketplace of Aksehir, a poor, shivering traveler walked past the steaming kitchen of a wealthy restaurant. The tavern master was boiling a giant cauldron of fragrant lamb broth seasoned with garlic, cinnamon, and cumin.

The penniless traveler pulled a dry crust of barley bread from his pocket and held it over the fragrant steam rising from the pot. He turned the bread around, inhaled the mouth-watering aroma deeply, and ate his softened crust with immense satisfaction.

Just as the poor man was about to walk away, the greedy restaurant owner leaped out of the shop, seized him by the collar, and roared: "Pay me five copper coins this instant!"

"For what, sir?" gasped the bewildered traveler. "I took not a single drop of your soup!"

"You nourished your bread with my rich steam!" barked the merchant. "The aroma belongs to my cauldron, and you have consumed its goodness!"

A crowd gathered, arguing loudly, when Mulla Nasruddin arrived riding his little gray donkey. Hearing the dispute, Nasruddin stroked his beard solemnly and announced: "Step aside, citizens! I shall adjudicate this case of high culinary jurisprudence!"

Nasruddin turned to the restaurant owner: "Is it true that this man ate the steam of your soup?"
"It is entirely true, Mulla!" cried the shopkeeper eagerly. "And steam costs good money to produce!"

Nasruddin reached deep into his pocket and pulled out five copper coins. He cupped the coins tightly inside his hands and shook them vigorously right next to the tavern master's ear: Jingle, jingle, clink!

"Do you hear that sound, tavern master?" asked Nasruddin with a serious frown.
"Of course I hear it, Mulla!" replied the greedy man. "What of it?"

"The judgment is settled!" proclaimed Nasruddin, pocketing the coins once more. "The sound of money pays in full for the smell of soup. Case dismissed!"

The crowd burst into uproarious laughter, while the greedy merchant slunk back into his shop, thoroughly outwitted by the Mulla's impeccable justice.
moral: A frivolous claim based on thin air deserves to be paid with nothing more than sound.

title: Who Stole the Smell?
full_text:
A baker who was notorious throughout the province for his extreme stinginess noticed that townsfolk often paused outside his bakery window in the early morning simply to enjoy the delicious fragrance of fresh baking bread.

Outraged that people were enjoying his merchandise without paying, the baker posted an armed guard at his door and brought a formal lawsuit before the town magistrate, charging thirty citizens with "stealing the fragrance of fresh rye."

The magistrate, completely baffled by the absurd complaint, summoned Mulla Nasruddin to give his opinion as the resident scholar.

Nasruddin listened with grave dignity. Then he asked the baker: "How much has your bakery's fragrance diminished because these poor people inhaled it?"

"Why, it hasn't diminished at all," stammered the baker. "The street still smells just as delicious!"

"Then by the ancient law of balance," declared Nasruddin, "the defendants must pay you with an equal portion of their shadows! Tomorrow at noon, when the sun is at its zenith, all thirty citizens shall stand in front of your shop window and allow you to look at their shadows for ten minutes. If you can bake bread with their shadows, you may keep them!"

The entire town square erupted in cheers, and the baker tore down his ridiculous lawsuit in utter embarrassment.
moral: Trying to hoard what nature gives freely makes one an object of public ridicule.

title: The Donkey and the Book
full_text:
Timur the Lame, the fierce conqueror, summoned Mulla Nasruddin to his grand pavilion. "Mulla," boomed the tyrant, "they say you are a teacher of miraculous wisdom. Can you teach my favorite donkey to read the great books of philosophy? If you succeed in ten years, I will grant you a chest of rubies; if you fail, you shall lose your head!"

Nasruddin bowed to the floor: "Sire, it shall be done! I require only ten years and a monthly stipend of gold to conduct the donkey's literary education."

When Nasruddin returned home leading the donkey, his terrified wife wept: "Are you insane, husband? How can an animal learn to read? In ten years you will be executed!"

"Be calm, my dear," smiled Nasruddin with a serene wink. "Ten years is a very long time! Within ten years, either Timur will die, or I will die, or the donkey will die! And in the meantime, we shall live comfortably on the royal stipend!"

Every day, Nasruddin hid grains of barley between the parchment pages of a large book. The donkey quickly learned to flip the pages with his tongue to eat the grains. When Nasruddin brought the donkey before the court, the beast eagerly turned the pages with his muzzle, braying loudly when no more barley was found.

"Look, Your Majesty!" exclaimed Nasruddin proudly. "The donkey has already mastered reading; he has completed chapter three and is now debating the author's logic!" Timur was so amused by the spectacle that he doubled the Mulla's reward.
moral: Flattering despots with impossible promises requires a long horizon and clever strategy.

title: The Lost Key
full_text:
Late one moonlit evening, several neighbors walking through the town square noticed Mulla Nasruddin down on all fours in the dust beneath a bright street lamp, searching frantically for something.

"What have you lost, Mulla?" asked a friendly neighbor, kneeling down to help him sift through the gravel.

"I have lost the iron key to my front door," replied Nasruddin, wiping sweat from his brow.

The neighbors immediately joined the search. For nearly an hour, five men crawled upon their hands and knees, combing through every pebble beneath the lamp, but not a trace of the key could be found.

Exhausted, one of the neighbors asked: "Mulla, are you absolutely sure you dropped the key here in the square?"

"Oh, no!" answered Nasruddin casually, pointing toward the dark alleyway twenty yards away. "I dropped it inside the dark coal-cellar behind my house!"

The neighbors stared at him in utter disbelief: "Then why in heaven's name are you searching for it out here under the street lamp?"

"Can you not see?" laughed Nasruddin with wide-eyed innocence. "It is pitch black in my cellar, whereas out here under the street lamp, there is plenty of light to see!"

The neighbors groaned, but Sufi masters smiled, knowing Nasruddin had just illustrated how mortals seek truth in the superficial glitter of the world rather than searching the deep, dark caverns of their own hearts.
moral: Searching for answers where it is convenient rather than where the truth was lost is human folly.

title: You Should Have Seen Me Before
full_text:
A group of strapping young wrestlers gathered in the village square, boasting of their mighty strength. One claimed he could lift an ox; another boasted he could uproot an olive tree.

Mulla Nasruddin, who was now well past seventy years of age with a snowy white beard and creaking joints, strode into the circle, puffing out his chest.

"You call that strength?" scoffed Nasruddin. "Why, I am just as strong today as I was when I was a fiery youth of twenty!"

The villagers were astonished. "Come now, Mulla!" said an elder. "How can an old man of seventy be as strong as a youth of twenty?"

"I have scientific proof!" declared Nasruddin proudly. "In my backyard stands an enormous stone boulder. When I was twenty years old, I tried with all my might to lift it, and I could not move it an inch. Yesterday morning, I tried with all my might to lift that very same boulder, and I still could not move it an inch! Therefore, my strength is exactly the same!"
moral: Boasting of lost youth only highlights the frailty of present vanity.

title: The Taste of the Same Donkey
full_text:
A traveling quack physician arrived in the village selling "Miraculous Elixir of Arabian Gazelle," claiming a single drop cured all ailments. He charged ten silver pieces per vial.

Nasruddin, suspecting a fraud, bought a vial, tasted a drop, and immediately spit it out: "Why, this is nothing but plain ditch water mixed with donkey vinegar!"

The quack became indignant: "How dare an ignorant villager insult imperial medicine! Bring me ten sick men, and I will prove its celestial potency!"

Nasruddin returned with his own wooden jug filled with water from his garden cistern. He had two villagers taste both the quack's potion and his own cistern water. Both villagers agreed that Nasruddin's water tasted much sweeter and fresher.

"You see?" announced Nasruddin to the crowd. "The quack sells sour donkey vinegar in gold vials, while my donkey gives pure spring water for free! Keep your silver coins in your pockets, and drink fresh water from your own wells!"
moral: Blind faith in labels often deceives people into accepting ordinary reality as magic.

title: The Coat Gets Invited
full_text:
A wealthy nobleman hosted a lavish banquet for the town dignitaries. Mulla Nasruddin, having worked all morning in his dusty vineyard, arrived at the palace in his worn, patched work clothes and mud-spattered boots.

The snobbish servants glanced at his rags and pushed him to the drafty corner near the kitchen door. The host walked past him without a word of greeting, and the waiters served him only cold broth and burnt crusts.

Nasruddin quietly slipped away, hurried home, and washed thoroughly. He put on his most magnificent holiday robe—a flowing kaftan of shimmering scarlet silk embroidered with gold thread and trimmed with luxurious fox fur—and donned a grand turban adorned with a silver brooch.

When he returned to the banquet hall, the servants bowed to the floor, opening the double doors with fanfare. The host rushed forward with open arms, embraced the Mulla, and seated him at the head of the banquet table upon velvet cushions.

Waiters immediately brought platters of roasted partridge, saffron pilaf, roasted almonds, and sweet pistachio halva.

Nasruddin smiled graciously. He picked up a spoonful of rich saffron stew and poured it directly into the sleeve of his silk robe! Then he dipped the fur hem of his kaftan into the almond sauce and rubbed sweet halva over his gold embroidery, murmuring affectionately: "Eat, my fine coat, eat! Enjoy the soup! Feast upon the pilaf!"

The host and guests were flabbergasted: "Mulla, what on earth are you doing? Why are you feeding your clothes?"

Nasruddin wiped his hands calmly and replied: "When I arrived an hour ago in my honest human body, wearing my working clothes, you turned me away into the cold corner. But when this coat arrived, you offered velvet cushions and royal delicacies! Therefore, it is obvious that this feast was prepared not for me, but for my coat! And it is only fair that the coat should enjoy what it has earned!"

The host blushed crimson with shame and apologized profusely, while the guests learned a lifelong lesson about the true worth of character over appearances.
moral: People who judge a man by his fine garments are entertaining clothes, not character.

title: How to Divide the Nuts
full_text:
Five boys were quarreling bitterly in the orchard over a sack of one hundred walnuts they had gathered. Unable to agree on a fair division, they saw Mulla Nasruddin approaching on his donkey and ran to him: "O wise Mulla! Please divide these walnuts among us fairly!"

Nasruddin sat down on a boulder and smiled: "Tell me, boys: do you wish me to divide these nuts according to human division, or according to God's division?"

The boys shouted eagerly: "According to God's division, Mulla! God's division must surely be the most perfect and sublime!"

"Very well," said Nasruddin.

He opened the sack. To the first boy, he gave seventy walnuts; to the second boy, he gave fifteen; to the third boy, he gave ten; to the fourth boy, he gave four; and to the fifth boy, he gave only one single wrinkled nut!

The boys were stunned and began to protest loudly: "Mulla! This is completely unfair! One boy got almost everything, and the last boy got almost nothing!"

Nasruddin stroked his beard with a twinkle in his eye: "Did you not ask for God's division? In this world, God gives boundless wealth to one man, a modest living to another, and poverty to a third, testing the generosity of the rich and the patience of the poor! If you had wanted an equal share for everyone, you should have asked for human division!"
moral: Human justice seeks fair equality; divine providence distributes according to mysterious design.

title: The Moon is More Useful
full_text:
In the lively teahouse of Akşehir, where village elders, traveling merchants, and amateur philosophers gathered every afternoon to debate under the shade of a venerable plane tree, a fierce philosophical argument broke out. Two visiting scholars with elaborate turbans were disputing whether the sun or the moon was the greater celestial blessing to mankind. One argued passionately that without the sun, all crops would wither and humanity would perish in perpetual frost; the other argued with equal vehemence that the moon governed the tides, guided desert caravans by night, and inspired poets. The debate grew so loud that the tea-server spilled a pot of boiling mint tea onto the hearth.

Looking across the cushions, the two scholars spotted Mulla Nasruddin sitting peacefully in the corner, gently blowing the steam from his tea glass with an expression of serene detachment. Recognizing him as the village judge, they cried out: "Come, Mulla! You are a man whose wits cut through confusion like a sharp blade. Settle this profound question for us: which is of greater utility and service to humanity—the radiant sun or the silvery moon?"

Nasruddin placed his glass carefully upon the copper tray, stroked his gray beard with profound gravity, and paused for a long moment while the whole teahouse leaned forward in silence. "Without a shadow of a doubt," declared Nasruddin with decisive authority, "the moon is infinitely more useful and necessary to mankind than the sun!" The scholars blinked in astonishment: "How in heaven's name do you arrive at such a strange conclusion, Mulla?" "The answer is obvious to anyone who uses simple common sense!" laughed Nasruddin, spreading his arms wide. "The sun shines exclusively during the daytime, when it is already broad daylight and nobody has any need of light at all! But the glorious moon shines in the middle of the pitch-black night, precisely when the world is dark and we desperately need illumination to keep from stumbling into ditches! Therefore, the moon is far superior!" The teahouse erupted into roars of laughter, leaving the two pompous scholars shaking their heads at how easily Nasruddin turned academic pretension upside down.
moral: People often undervalue constant blessings while praising what arrives in moments of darkness.

title: Nasruddin's Donkey is Dead?
full_text:
One dusty morning in Akşehir, Mulla Nasruddin was seen sprinting into the crowded market square, his turban askew, his robes flapping in the wind, clapping his hands together and shouting at the top of his lungs: "Praise be to the Almighty! Glory to the Heavens! What a boundless miracle of divine mercy and blessings has fallen upon my humble head today!"

The merchants stopped measuring cloth, the blacksmith dropped his tongs, and Nasruddin’s neighbor ran over in great excitement, clutching the Mulla’s shoulder: "What magnificent fortune has befallen you, Mulla? Did an uncle in Samarkand pass away and leave you a chest of jewels? Did you dig up a pot of gold beneath your olive tree?" "No, no, nothing of the sort!" beamed Nasruddin, his eyes shining with radiant joy. "My faithful gray donkey broke its tether this morning, galloped wild toward the cliffs, tumbled into the rocky ravine, and broke its neck on the boulders below!"

The neighbor stared at him as if he had lost his senses: "Are you completely mad, Mulla Nasruddin? You have lost your only beast of burden, the animal that plows your patch of barley and carries your firewood to the bazaar! Why on earth are you running through the square thanking heaven that your only donkey is dead?" "O man of small understanding!" laughed Nasruddin, shaking his head with affectionate pity. "Can you not perceive the boundless miracle? I am thanking heaven with all my soul that I was not riding on its back when it tumbled into the abyss! Had I been sitting in the saddle, I would have broken my neck along with the poor beast! A lost donkey can be replaced with fifty silver coins, but where in all Anatolia could my dear wife find another Mulla Nasruddin?" The crowd chuckled at his irrepressible optimism, marveling at how a cheerful spirit finds reasons for gratitude even in the midst of loss.
moral: Finding reasons for gratitude even in misfortune preserves a cheerful spirit.

title: Whose Voice?
full_text:
A neighbor who was notoriously careless with borrowed tools knocked on Nasruddin's door: "Mulla, lend me your donkey for the afternoon; I must carry timber from the forest."

Nasruddin, who knew the neighbor never fed borrowed animals, replied from inside: "I would gladly lend it to you, my dear friend, but alas, my donkey is not here today; my son took it to the neighboring town at dawn."

Just at that moment, the donkey brayed loudly from inside the stable: "Hee-haw! Hee-haw!"

The neighbor became indignant: "Shame on you, Mulla! You tell me the donkey is in the neighboring town, when I can hear it braying with my own ears right inside your stable!"

Nasruddin stepped onto the porch, looking at the neighbor with offended dignity: "My good man! Whom do you choose to believe: an honorable scholar with a gray beard who speaks the truth, or an ignorant donkey?"
moral: Believing an animal's noise over the reasoned word of a friend exposes shallow faith.

title: The Borrowed Pot
full_text:
Mulla Nasruddin borrowed a large bronze cooking pot from his wealthy, greedy neighbor to prepare a family feast. A week later, he returned the pot, but inside it rested a tiny little copper pot.

The neighbor was puzzled: "Mulla, what is this tiny pot doing inside my cauldron?"

"Rejoice, neighbor!" whispered Nasruddin solemnly. "While your pot was in my kitchen, it became pregnant and gave birth to this delightful little child! And since you own the mother, the child belongs to you by law!"

The greedy neighbor laughed to himself, thinking Nasruddin was a simpleton, and happily kept both pots.

A month later, Nasruddin came back and borrowed the big cauldron again. Weeks passed, and Nasruddin did not return it. Finally, the neighbor marched to Nasruddin's house, demanding: "Where is my cooking pot, Mulla?"

Nasruddin wiped away a tear: "Alas, my dear neighbor! I bring you tragic news! Your beloved bronze pot has passed away; it died peacefully in my kitchen yesterday, and I buried it with full honors."

"Are you out of your mind?" screamed the furious neighbor. "How can a bronze cooking pot die?"

"Come now, neighbor," smiled Nasruddin calmly. "You were perfectly willing to believe that your pot could give birth to a baby; why then can you not believe that it can die? Whatever is born must surely one day taste death!"
moral: If you accept an impossible gain based on greed, you must also accept the impossible loss.

title: The Longer Beard
full_text:
One Friday afternoon, the courtyard of the grand mosque in Akşehir was filled with merchants, village elders, and eager students who had gathered to listen to a visiting scholar from the renowned academies of Baghdad. The visitor was a man of immense pomposity, adorned in shimmering silk robes trimmed with golden embroidery, and possessed an extraordinary white beard that cascaded down his chest in glorious waves, reaching all the way to his leather belt. He stroked his facial hair with supreme complacency, pausing after every sentence with a solemn air as though the heavens themselves hung upon his words.

Addressing the humble congregation with an air of condescending superiority, the scholar cleared his throat and declared: "O seekers of knowledge, let it be known that true dignity, depth of scholarship, and spiritual authority are strictly proportional to the length and fullness of a man’s beard! The longer and grander the beard, the deeper and more profound the ocean of divine wisdom that resides in the intellect beneath!" The villagers bowed their heads in bewildered awe, murmuring respectfully among themselves, too intimidated to question the distinguished guest.

From the back of the crowd, Mulla Nasruddin quietly rose to his feet, his worn felt cap slightly tilted and his fingers casually stroking his own short, modest gray beard. "Respected master," called out Nasruddin with profound gravity, bowing low with mock reverence. "Your revolutionary doctrine brings boundless illumination to our simple minds. For if wisdom, dignity, and religious authority were truly measured by the length of the hair upon one’s chin, then without a shadow of a doubt, the village billy goat tethered behind the blacksmith’s shop must be the Supreme Grand Mufti of the entire Islamic world!" The entire courtyard burst into uncontrollable laughter, while the Baghdad scholar hurriedly gathered his silk robes and vanished down the street in red-faced silence.
moral: Measuring wisdom by the length of a beard mistakes outward hair for inner intellect.

title: Half Knowledge

One afternoon, a haughty grammarian from the imperial capital stepped into his wooden skiff. As Nasruddin pulled steadily at the heavy oars, pushing against the frothing current, the scholar adjusted his spectacles, sneered at the Mulla’s calloused hands, and asked in a condescending voice: "Tell me, ferryman, have you ever studied the intricate rules of Arabic grammar, syntax, and classical rhetoric?"

I know how to mend an oar, read the river eddies, and haul cargo, but I have never opened a book of grammar in my life." The scholar shook his head with theatrical sorrow and announced loudly so the other passengers could hear: "What a tragedy! You have lived like a beast in the dark! In that case, my poor man, at least half of your entire life has been completely wasted!"

Just as the scholar finished speaking, a violent mountain squall swept down the gorge. A monstrous wave slammed against the side of the skiff, snapping the steering rudder and smashing a hole through the floorboards. As icy water rushed into the boat and it began to sink rapidly beneath the white foam, the passengers screamed in terror. Nasruddin dropped his oars, stripped off his heavy coat, and turned to the trembling professor, who was clutching his parchment scrolls with white knuckles. "Professor," shouted Nasruddin above the roar of the water, "have you ever in your life studied the practical science of swimming?" "No, alas, heavens preserve me, never!" shrieked the petrified grammarian. "Then, my dear professor," shouted Nasruddin as he dove gracefully into the river, "your whole life has been completely wasted, for this boat is going straight to the bottom!"

title: The Hot Soup and Cold Winter
full_text:
The village elders bet Nasruddin that he could not spend an entire freezing winter night on the snowy mountain peak without a fire, coat, or blanket. If he survived, they would buy him a grand feast.

Nasruddin accepted the wager, stood on the freezing summit all night, and survived by watching a tiny candle flame flickering in a farmhouse window a mile away.

The next morning, the greedy elders refused to pay: "You warmed yourself by the candle light a mile away! You lost the bet!"

Nasruddin said nothing. He invited them to dinner that evening. The guests arrived hungry, but after two hours, no food appeared. Looking into the kitchen, they saw Nasruddin holding a giant cauldron of soup suspended from the ceiling, with a tiny candle burning on the floor five feet below it!

"Mulla, are you crazy?" shouted the elders. "How can a candle five feet below boil a giant pot?"

"If a tiny candle a mile away could keep me warm through a winter blizzard," replied Nasruddin, "it can surely boil your soup in a few days! Sit down and wait!"

The ashamed elders apologized and paid the bet in full.
moral: Technical hair-splitting used to deny a fair reward deserves an equally absurd response.

title: The Sermon
full_text:
Mounting the pulpit on Friday, Nasruddin asked the congregation: "Do you know what I am going to speak about today?"

"No, Mulla!" replied the crowd.
"If you do not know, I have no desire to waste words on such ignorant people!" said Nasruddin, and he stepped down and went home.

The next Friday, he asked the same question. The people, determined not to be dismissed, replied: "Yes, Mulla, we know!"
"If you already know," said Nasruddin, "there is no need for me to tell you!" And he departed once more.

On the third Friday, the people agreed among themselves: half would answer "Yes" and half would answer "No."

Nasruddin asked: "Do you know what I am going to speak about?"
Half the congregation cried "Yes!" and half cried "No!"

Nasruddin beamed with delight: "Splendid! Then let those who know tell those who do not!" And he walked out into the sunshine.
moral: Teaching that relies on the community to enlighten one another achieves true harmony.

title: The Cat Ate the Meat
full_text:
Nasruddin bought three pounds of prime lamb at the bazaar, carried it home, and told his wife: "Prepare a rich meat stew for tonight; I have invited several honored friends."

While Nasruddin was at the mosque, his wife cooked the delicious stew, but could not resist tasting a piece. One piece led to another, and soon she and her gossiping neighbors had eaten every single scrap of the meat.

When Nasruddin returned with his hungry guests, his wife pretended to weep: "Alas, husband! A catastrophe! While I turned my back, your greedy black cat leaped onto the stove and ate all three pounds of lamb!"

Nasruddin did not raise his voice. He quietly picked up the black cat, carried it to the apothecary's shop next door, and placed it on the merchant's brass scale.

The weights balanced at exactly three pounds!

Nasruddin turned to his blushing wife with a serious frown: "My dear, if this three pounds of flesh on the scale is the cat—then where on earth is the meat? And if this is the meat—then where on earth is the cat?"
moral: Transparent lies crumble before the simplest test of logic.
